self-explain connections among multiple visual representations. They compared students who learned with T+MV representations with such connectional-understanding support to students who learned with T+MV representations without such support. Results showed higher learning outcomes on a content knowledge test for students who received connectional-understanding support. Gutwill et al. (1999) tested the effects of connectional-understanding support that provided step-by-step guidance to find corresponding features in different visual representations. Students with connectional-understanding support showed higher learning of content knowledge than students in a control group without connectional-understanding support. In a qualitative study, Linenberger and Bretz (2012) provided connectional-understanding support via teacher questions that asked students to explain differences between visual representations. Based on an analysis of interviews and student-teacher dialogue, they argue that connectional-understanding support enhanced students’ learning of the content knowledge.

Further, direct evidence for hypothesis 2 comes from experiments showing that students learning with T+MV representations outperform students learning with T+SV representations only if they receive connectional-understanding support. Rau et al. (2012) compared students learning with T+MV representations who received connectional-understanding support in the form of self-explanation prompts to students learning with T+MV representations without such support and to students learning with T+SV representations. Results showed that only students who received connectional-understanding support outperformed the T+SV condition.

Finally, indirect evidence for hypothesis 2 comes from research showing that connectional understanding is a prerequisite for students’ acquisition of other representational competencies that facilitate students’ learning of content knowledge, specifically of connectional fluency. Rau and colleagues (2013b; Rau, Making connections in chemistry: How does learning to explicitly compare visual representations relate to learning to automatically classify representations?, under review) tested different sequences of instructional support for connectional understanding and for connectional fluency. Students who received connectionalunderstanding support benefited more from subsequent connectional-fluency support than students who had not previously received connectional-understanding support. Further, students with low prior connectional understanding did not benefit from connectional-fluency support unless they also received connectional-understanding support (Rau, Making connections in chemistry: How does learning to explicitly compare visual representations relate to learning to automatically classify representations?, under review).

In summary, there is mostly indirect and some direct evidence for hypothesis 2. Taken together, research suggests that T+MV scenarios are more effective than T+SV scenarios particularly if students have acquired or receive instructional support for connectional understanding. Further, students can acquire connectional understanding while they learn content knowledge if they receive instructional support to make sense of the connections. For example, we may expect that the T+MV scenario (Fig. 1c) is more effective than the T+SV scenario (Fig. 1b) if students receive support to reason about which visual features of the pie chart correspond to which visual features in the rectangle and the numberline.
Hypothesis 3: Visual Fluency

Based on the rationale that visual fluency may play a more important role as a facilitator of students’ learning in T+MV than in T+SV scenarios, hypothesis 3 suggests that an advantage of T+MV scenarios over T+SV scenarios is more pronounced if students (1) have prior visual fluency, or (2) receive instructional support for visual fluency.

Indirect empirical evidence for hypothesis 3 comes from studies on students who lack visual fluency in T+SV and T+MV scenarios. Even if students have visual understanding, working with them may require considerable cognitive effort and may involve ineffective visual search processes. Eye-tracking studies indicate that visually fluent students are more efficient at allocating visual attention to relevant visual features (for an overview, see Gegenfurtner et al. 2011). For example, Carmichael et al. (2010) found that experts direct their attention to conceptually relevant features of visual representations, whereas novices tend to focus on salient surface features. These eye-gaze measures correlated with students performance in using the visual representations to solve domain-relevant tasks.

Further indirect support for hypothesis 3 comes from research on connection making among visual representations. Recall that visual fluency frees cognitive resources that students can invest into connection making among visual representations. Hinze et al. (2013a) investigated whether fluency with a familiar visual representation affects adoption of a new visual representation. Eye-gaze data showed that students who are fluent with the familiar visual representation more readily adopted the new visual representation. Arguably, students learned about the new visual representation by connecting it to the familiar visual representation.

Finally, indirect support for hypothesis 3 comes from studies on instructional support for visual fluency in T+MV scenarios. Such instructional support exposes students to numerous example representations designed so that students are likely to induce which visual features are relevant, for example by providing contrasting cases (Massey et al. 2011) or by interleaving relevant features (Rau et al. 2014). Kellman and colleagues developed visual-fluency supports that provide students with many short tasks that ask them to rapidly translate between multiple external representations. For example, a student might be asked to select one of several pie charts that correspond to a word problem. The task sequences are designed to expose students to systematic variation, often in the form of contrasting cases, so that irrelevant features vary but relevant features appear across several tasks (Kellman and Massey 2013; Massey et al. 2011). Kellman and colleagues evaluated this type of visual-fluency support in a number of controlled experiments and observational studies in T+MV scenarios for several domains, including algebra, fractions, and chemistry (Kellman et al. 2009; Kellman et al. 2008; Wise et al. 2000). Results showed that visual-fluency support led to large and lasting gains on tests of visual fluency. Furthermore, gains in visual fluency were associated with higher learning outcomes on content knowledge tests. Other forms of visual-fluency support, such as interleaving sequences of visual representations so that students encounter a different type of visual representation in consecutive tasks (Rau et al. 2014) and use them for different task types (Rau et al. 2013a), have also been shown to enhance learning of content knowledge.

In sum, there is indirect evidence in support of hypothesis 3, which suggests that T+MV scenarios are more effective than T+SV scenarios particularly if students have acquired or receive instructional support for visual fluency. While students can acquire visual fluency through extensive practice, targeted trainings have also shown to be effective. Therefore, we may for example expect that a student who is fluent with pie charts but not with rectangles and numberlines might benefit more from the T+SV scenario (Fig. 1b) than from the T+MV scenario (Fig. 1c) if he/she receives additional support for visual fluency with rectangles and numberlines. However, a direct experimental test of hypothesis 3 is still outstanding.
Hypothesis 4: Connectional Fluency
Based on the argument that connectional fluency is a facilitator of students’ learning in T+MV scenarios (but not in T+SV scenarios), hypothesis 4 suggests that an advantage of T+MV

scenarios over T+SV scenarios is more pronounced if students (1) have prior connectional fluency for the visual representations or (2) receive instructional support for connectional fluency.

Indirect evidence for hypothesis 4 comes from studies by Kellman and colleagues who developed connectional-fluency supports that ask students to rapidly translate among visual representations (Kellman et al. 2009; Massey et al. 2011; Wise et al. 2000). For example, students may select one of several numberlines that show the same fraction as a pie chart. Experiments show that such connectional-fluency supports enhance learning of content knowledge in a variety of domains (Kellman et al. 2009; Kellman et al. 2008; Wise et al. 2000).

Direct evidence for hypothesis 4 comes from an experiment that compared learning with T+ MV representations with or without connectional-fluency support to learning with T+SV representations (Rau et al. 2012). In this study, students learned about fractions using pie charts, rectangles, and numberlines. Only students who received connectional-fluency support showed higher learning gains in content knowledge than the T+SV condition. Follow-up studies suggested that connectional understanding and connectional fluency are indeed separate representational competencies that are best supported by different types of instructional interventions. Rau et al. (2012) and Rau and Wu (2015) found that students who received both connectional-fluency support (designed to engage nonverbal inductive learning processes) and connectional-understanding support (designed to engage verbally mediated sense-making processes) showed higher learning gains on content knowledge tests than students who received either type of support alone.

In sum, although most of the evidence for hypothesis 4 is indirect, there is some emerging direct evidence in support of hypothesis 4. Taken together, this evidence suggests that T+MV scenarios are more effective than T+SV scenarios particularly if students have acquired or receive instructional support for connectional fluency. While students can acquire connectional fluency through extensive practice in translating across multiple visual representations, targeted trainings have also shown to be effective. Therefore, we may, for example expect that the T+MV scenario (Fig. 1c) is more effective than the T+SV scenario (Fig. 1b) if students are fluent in translating among the pie chart, rectangle, and numberline representations.
Hypothesis 5: Meta-Representational Competencies

Based on the argument that the higher complexity of meta-representational decisions in T+MV than in T+SV scenarios implies that the role of meta-representational competencies is more important in T+MV than in T+SV scenarios, hypothesis 5 states that an advantage of T+MV scenarios over T+SV scenarios is more pronounced if students (1) have prior metarepresentational competencies, or (2) receive instructional support for them.

Indirect evidence for this hypothesis comes from studies showing that choosing inappropriate visual representations for a learning activity may jeopardize the students’ learning of content knowledge (Gruber et al. 1995; Schnotz and Bannert 2003; Yerushamly 1991). Therefore, if students choose their visual representations themselves, making inappropriate choices may equally jeopardize their learning success. Students’ difficulties in choosing visual representations are well documented: students vary largely in their ability to select (Roberts et al. 1997) or construct (Cox and Brna 1995) visual representations that are appropriate for a task, and they often fail to select the appropriate visual representation to solve a given task (Uesaka and Manalo 2006).

Additional indirect evidence comes from research on instructional support for metarepresentational competencies in T+MV scenarios. For example, Uesaka and Manalo (2006) showed that asking students to compare visual representations resulted in more appropriate representational choices and higher learning outcomes on a content knowledge test, compared to a control condition without such support. Grawemeyer (2006) evaluated an educational technology that supports students in choosing appropriate visual representations for a given task. Results showed that students improved their performance on a content knowledge test. Acevedo Nistal et al. (2015) tested a type of support that helped students match representational choices to task demands and to personal characteristics. Students who received this type of support made more adaptive representational choices and showed higher outcomes on a content knowledge test, compared to a control group without such support. However, because these studies did not involve a T+SV control condition, they did not directly test hypothesis 5.

In sum, there is indirect evidence for hypothesis 5, suggesting that an advantage of T+MV over T+SV scenarios is more pronounced if students have acquired or receive instructional support for meta-representational competencies. For example, the T+MV scenario (Fig. 1c) may be more effective than the T+SV scenario (Fig. 1b) if a student knows to select the pie chart for task 1 because it matches the pizza scenario and the numberline for task 3 because it matches the distance scenario. However, a formal test of his hypothesis 5 is outstanding.
Hypothesis 6: Information Overlap

Above, it was argued that information from irrelevant or unrelated visual representations cannot be integrated into a correct mental model, and that integrating information from redundant visual representations is cognitively demanding but does not yield additional insight. Based on this argument, hypothesis 6 suggests that an advantage of T+MV scenarios over T+SV scenarios is more pronounced if each visual representation provides information about the learning content that (1) adds relevant information not fully covered by the other visual representations but (2) overlaps partially with information provided in the other visual representations.

Indirect evidence for this claim comes from studies on T+SV scenarios that have considered whether the visual representation provides information that is relevant to the learning task (e.g., Carney and Levin 2002; Schnotz and Bannert 2003). For example, Schnotz and Bannert (2003) compared a text-only condition to two T+SV representations conditions in which the visual representation either did or did not align with the demands of the learning task. T+SV representations resulted in higher learning outcomes than text-only if the visual representation aligned with the task demands. Otherwise, the visual representation interfered with learning of content knowledge. Further, a study showing that T+SV representations can have a negative effect for students if the visual representation shows irrelevant information (Magner et al. 2012) can be interpreted as support for hypothesis 6. In this study, negative effects of irrelevant visual representations were limited to low-prior knowledge students. It is possible that lowprior knowledge students did not realize that the visual representations were not useful, and hence tried to attempt to integrate them with the text. Even though these studies were conducted in T+SV scenarios, these effects should generalize to T+MV scenarios.

Further indirect evidence for hypothesis 6 comes from research on information overlap among multiple visual representations in T+MV scenarios. Studies by Ainsworth et al. (2002) and by Bodner and Domin (2000) found that T+MV representations did not result in higher learning outcomes than T+SV representations if one visual representation provided all necessary information. Considering the variability of visual representations in experiments that

failed to show an advantage of T+MV representations over T+SV representations can also be interpreted as supporting hypothesis 6 (Berthold and Renkl 2009; Corradi et al. 2012; Rau et al. 2012, 2015a). In these studies, visual representations in the T+MV conditions did not differ on dimensions of concreteness or interactivity; all visual representations were abstract and virtual. It is possible that visual representations that differ on these dimensions have less information overlap than visual representations that do not. Hence, multiple visual representations that differ on these design dimensions may have a higher pay-off than multiple visual representations that do not differ on these dimensions (Carney and Levin 2002). Indeed, there is considerable evidence for the effectiveness of combining visual representations that differ on these dimensions. For example, combining concrete and abstract visual representations (Braithwaite and Goldstone 2013; Fyfe et al. 2014; McNeil and Fyfe 2012; Moreno et al. 2011), and combining physical and virtual representations (Olympiou and Zacharia 2012; Zacharia et al. 2008) was shown to be more effective than T+MV representations that were only abstract, only concrete, only physical, or only virtual. Yet, because these studies did not include a T+SV control condition, they did not directly test hypothesis 6.

In sum, there is indirect evidence in support of hypothesis 6, suggesting that T+MV scenarios are more effective than T+SV scenarios if each added visual representation contributes information that is relevant to the learning task and overlaps to a medium degree with information shown in other visual representations. For example, we may expect the T+MV scenario (Fig. 1c) to be more effective than the T+SV scenario (Fig. 1b) only if the numberline provides information about the sharing tasks that is not captured by the pie chart and the rectangle. However, a direct test of hypothesis 6 is still outstanding.
Hypothesis 7: Socio-Cultural Conventions

Based on the socio-cultural perspective that the goal of education is to enable students to participate in practices common in scientific and professional communities, hypothesis 7 suggests that T+MV scenarios are more effective than T+SV scenarios if the use of each visual representation aligns with its use in the target community of practice. Specifically, this perspective suggests that we need to consider how social and cultural conventions affect representational competencies (Rau et al. 2015b). In particular, we may need to consider the following:
Which visual representations students are exposed to (i.e., the fact that students use multiple visual representations in the first place)
– How the visual representations are to be interpreted (i.e., visual understanding)
What level of fluency in using the representation is desirable and how it is to be assessed (i.e., visual fluency)
What connections students are asked to make among specific visual representations (i.e., connectional understanding)
To what extent it is necessary to be able to fluently translate among specific visual representations (i.e., connectional fluency)

Which visual representations are deemed to be suitable for which types of tasks, and whether there are predicated preferences for one visual representation over the other (i.e., meta-representational competencies)
To the best of my knowledge, there is no empirical research that explicitly tested hypothesis 7. Yet, indirect evidence can be obtained by comparing the use of visual representations in

Fractions in Mathematics: Promoting Abstract Understanding

Fractions are an inherently difficult topic for elementary school students because they encompass many concepts, including parts of a whole (Cramer and Henry 2002; Cramer and Wyberg 2009), measurement (Carpenter 1971), ratios (Fuson and Abrahamson 2005; Lamon 1999), equipartitioning (Confrey and Maloney 2010), as well as units and re-unitizing (Cramer and Henry 2002; Cramer and Wyberg 2009; Lamon 1999; Yanik et al. 2008). Different visual representations emphasize different conceptual interpretations of fractions (Charalambous and Pitta-Pantazi 2007). Commonly used visual representations of fractions include area models that help students understand equi-partitioning and parts-of-a-whole concepts (e.g., pie chart, rectangles), linear models that highlight measurement concepts (e.g., fraction strips, numberlines), and discrete models that emphasize ratio interpretations (e.g., sets, counters). Instruction often starts out by using concrete representations (e.g., pictures of pizzas) and physical representations (e.g., real pizzas) in order to ground student’s visual understanding in concrete experiences (e.g., sharing activities; (Cramer and Wyberg 2009; Moss 2005; Proctor et al. 2002).

Connectional understanding is considered key to students’ fractions learning (NCTM 2000, 2006; NMAP 2008; Siegler et al. 2010; Thompson and Saldanha 2003). Hence, instruction typically supports students in making connections by mapping conceptually relevant features across representations (e.g., by mapping the numerator shown by a shaded section in a pie chart to the number of sections between 0 and a dot on a numberline). Ultimately, the goal of connection making is to help students gain abstract understanding of fractions as proportions of a unit and to promote understanding of the symbolic notation of fractions and decimals (Hecht et al. 2007; Miura and Yamagishi 2002). Indeed, supports for promoting connectional fluency have been shown to enhance students learning of fractions (Kellman et al. 2008; Rau et al. 2012). However, connectional fluency serves as a means to an end in enhancing students’ implicit understanding of abstract proportions, rather than being an end in and of itself. In the same way, meta-representational competencies play less of a role in fractions expertise. Students may learn that a pie chart is more appropriate than a numberline when it comes to depicting sharing scenarios. Yet, this is not a decision a mathematics expert typically faces; mathematics experts typically rely on symbols (Kieren 1993) and one dominant visual representation: coordinate systems (Even 1998; Janvier et al. 1993), which build on knowledge about numberline representations (Siegler et al. 2010).

Thus, fractions is a domain in which the processes involved in learning with T+MV representations is mainly instrumental to enhancing students’ learning of abstract concepts so that they can come to rely on symbols and coordinate systems when they become experts.
Bonding in Chemistry: Communicating About Concepts

Students struggle with crucial chemistry concepts related to bonding across high school, undergraduate, and graduate levels (Cooper et al. 2012; Nicoll 2001; Talanquer 2006). These difficulties result from the fact that many key concepts cannot be observed with the regular eye (Davidowitz and Chittleborough 2009) and are inherently abstract (Justi and Gilbert 2002). Different visual representations provide complementary views on these concepts (Bodner and Domin 2000; Coll and Treagust 2003; Kozma and Russell 2005). Relying on only one visual

representation can severely interfere with students’ learning (Furio et al. 2000; Gabel and Bunce 1994). For example, to understand how atoms bond to form molecules, students typically encounter the visual representations shown in Fig. 2: they need to understand which atoms participate in the bonds (Lewis structures), bond angles and molecular volume (balland-stick models and space-filling models), and the distribution of electrons across the molecule (electronic potential maps) (Bowen 1990; Hinze et al. 2013b; Shusterman and Shusterman 1997). Chemistry experts have sophisticated mental models of which visual representation depicts information necessary for a given task (Kozma and Russell 2005).

In contrast to the fractions example, chemistry experts heavily rely on visual representations to solve chemistry tasks (Kozma and Russell 1997). Hence, the goal in using T+MV representations in chemistry instruction is not only to promote abstract understanding of the content, but also to promote students’ learning of a Bvisual language^ (Kozma and Russell 2005; Taber 2013). In addition, the chemistry education literature emphasizes the importance of becoming fluent in using individual visual representations (i.e., visual fluency) and in readily and effortlessly translating among multiple visual representations (i.e., connectional fluency; (Hinze et al. 2013a; Justi et al. 2009). In addition, meta-representational competencies are considered an important learning goal in and of itself: students need to learn which visual representation depicts which particular concepts, and when depicting these specific concepts is important for the given task (Gilbert 2005; Justi et al. 2009; Kozma and Russell 2005).

It is also important to note that some of visual representations in chemistry have significant information overlap, for example, ball-and-stick models and space-filling models depict atoms as spheres that correspond to their molecular volume, and both depict bond angles. They differ only with respect to how salient they make these two aspects: ball-and-stick models make it easier to see bond angles and bond types, whereas space-filling models make it easier to see the molecular volume. Because both are used in chemistry communities of practice, students typically encounter both ball-and-stick models and space-filling models during instruction.

A further goal in chemistry education is to understand the role of historical visual representations that are no longer used by experts. These visual representations are no longer in use because they have proven inaccurate (e.g., Bohr models that show electrons as orbiting a nucleus). Yet, they remain important because they had a significant impact on scientific discoveries in chemistry (e.g., on electrostatic forces) (Gabel and Bunce 1994; Nakiboglu 2003; Rocke 2010). Thus, chemistry is a domain in which representational competencies are a crucial aspect of domain expertise. Hence, the acquisition of representational competencies is a goal in and of itself.
Summary

This comparison illustrates that the role of particular representational competencies in education differs between the fractions and chemistry domains, and that these differences align with the socio-cultural practices of the use of visual representations in these domains. In comparison

Discussion and Future Directions

The goal of this article was to investigate under which conditions T+MV may be more effective than T+SV scenarios in enhancing learning of content knowledge. This article approached this question from the perspective of the representation dilemma; that is, it investigated how students can learn about visual representations (i.e., acquiring representational competencies) while learning from visual representations (i.e., acquiring content knowledge). To this end, this article reviewed which representational competencies are involved in students’ learning of content knowledge (Table 1). Two conceptual representational competencies acquired via verbally mediated sense-making processes were identified: visual understanding, connectional understanding. Two perceptual representational competencies acquired via nonverbal inductive learning processes were identified: visual understanding and visual fluency. Finally, meta-representational competencies build on both conceptual and perceptual competencies. Second, focusing on learning processes allowed analyzing how the number of visual representations affects the role these representational competencies play during students’ learning of content knowledge. Specifically, contrasting T+SV and T+MV scenarios revealed that visual understanding is a facilitator of students’ learning in T+SV scenarios, but a necessary prerequisite for learning in T+MV scenarios. Visual fluency plays a stronger role as a facilitator in T+MV scenarios. Connectional understanding and connectional fluency are facilitators of learning only in T+MV scenarios. Meta-representational competencies are more complex in T+MV than in T+SV scenarios and may therefore be a more important facilitator of students’ learning in T+MV than in T+SV scenarios. This comparison yielded seven hypotheses that specify when T+MV scenarios might be more effective than T+SV scenarios. Empirical evidence for each of these hypotheses was reviewed (Table 2).

This review suggests several open questions that should be addressed in future research. First, it is worth noting that most support for these hypotheses comes from indirect evidence. Future experiments should empirically test these hypotheses in a variety of domains.

Furthermore, the hypotheses emerged from considerations about how conceptual and perceptual representational competencies interact with one another. However, we still know relatively little about these interactions. There are at least six important interactions that we

should investigate in future research. First, we need to investigate interactions between sensemaking processes and inductive learning processes in order to provide effective instructional support that helps students benefit from T+MV representations. For example, if connectional fluency requires that students have connectional understanding, we may have to provide connectional-understanding support before connectional-fluency support. We know little about these interactions because research on sense-making of concepts and inductive learning of perceptual knowledge has been separate in the area of multiple external representations. This separation is somewhat surprising because there is a longstanding tradition in other areas of cognitive psychology to investigate relations between perceptual learning and conceptual learning (Goldstone and Barsalou 1998; Goldstone et al. 1997). In general, research on learning with visual representations would benefit from integrating these two perspectives. In particular, given the larger role of perceptual competencies for T+MV scenarios, integrating perceptual learning perspective into this research may yield interesting insights into differences between T+SV and T+MV scenarios.

Second, we need to investigate how processes of using individual visual representations interact with processes of connection making among visual representations. It was argued that visual understanding and fluency can promote connection making, while connectional understanding and fluency can also promote visual understanding and fluency. An open question is how much prior visual understanding is necessary so that a student can benefit from connection making tasks. Is a minimal level of visual understanding sufficient in enabling students to make connections? Or is a high level of visual fluency in at least one visual representation necessary, so that students can learn a second visual representation through connection making?

Third, it was argued that meta-representational competencies build on visual understanding, visual fluency, connectional understanding, and connectional fluency. However, it is an open question to what extent these representational competencies are required for the acquisition of meta-representational competencies, and whether teaching students about metarepresentational competencies can enhance acquisition of other representational competencies as well. One important open question is how the student’s prior representational competencies interact with their students’ goals when acquiring meta-representational competencies. For example, it may matter whether the student prioritizes learning goals versus performance goals (Pintrich 2000). A student with performance goals may always choose the visual representation he/she is most fluent with because this choice will most likely lead to success in problem solving. In contrast, a student with learning goals may be more willing to choose the visual representation he/she is less fluent with because this choice has the highest pay-off in terms of learning gains. Should instructional support for meta-representational competencies take students’ learning goals into account, and—if so—how? Another open question is whether students need connectional understanding before they can benefit from instructional support for meta-representational competencies. As mentioned above, support for meta-representational competence may enhance students’ understanding of connections because it requires students to reflect on the differences between visual representations. However, comparing visual representations is cognitively demanding and may lead to cognitive overload unless students have at least some prior level of conceptual understanding. Yet, we still know little about what level of prior connectional understanding is necessary for students’ benefit from support for metarepresentational competencies.

Fourth, when we consider interactions among representational competencies, we need to take into account that they are socially mediated and shaped by socio-cultural conventions. As argued above, the relative importance of representational competencies is defined by the practices of the target community. From a socio-cultural perspective, the goal of instruction is to enable students to become part of scientific and professional communities, which implies that instructional interventions should reflect the cultural conventions and social functions the visual representations serve in the target community. More research is needed to investigate how practices in expert communities affect instructional support for learning with multiple visual representations.

For educational psychologists, incorporating a socio-cultural perspective would require that we understand how visual representations are used within the target community. This involves considerable effort: we have to delve deeply into discipline-based literatures that describe the educational goals with which visual representations are used. It would be helpful for the educational psychology research community to consolidate such discipline-based literatures into an overview across potential target domains. Such an overview would allow our research community to investigate in what ways socio-cultural aspects affect the generalizability of our findings about learning with multiple visual representations. Such an overview would also be useful to make predictions as to which types of instructional support for representational processes may be most effective for a given target domain. For example, based on the educational psychology literature, we might predict that students may not benefit from multiple visual representations if they have considerable information overlap, because the benefits (e.g., little additional information) do not outweigh the costs (e.g., effort necessary to make connections). Therefore, we may recommend using only one visual representation in instruction. Yet, if experts in the target community use different visual representations that have considerable information overlap, it is still necessary that students who are trained to become part of that community learn with these visual representations. In this case, we may recommend different types of instruction for different students. Those students who aim for a career in the discipline (e.g., biology majors) should learn with T+MV representations, and they should receive appropriate instructional supports (see section 5). Students who do not aim for a career in the given domain (e.g., nonscience majors in a science course) may benefit more from T+SV than T+MV representations. To date, it remains an open question how best to map requirements that result from discipline-specific practices to instructional interventions that are based on educational psychology research.

Fifth, it is still an open question to what extent representational competencies transfer across representations (NRC 2006). This review suggests that visual understanding and connectional understanding may transfer to visual representations that have similar featurereferent mappings (Gentner et al. 2003). Based on this argument, it was suggested that those competencies that result from sense-making processes (i.e., visual and connectional understanding, meta-representational knowledge) may transfer more easily than those that result from inductive processes (i.e., visual and connectional fluency), because sense-making processes involve principle-based reasoning and structure mapping, whereas inductive processes involve experience-based learning that is not verbally mediated. In contrast, visual fluency and connectional fluency may not transfer to novel visual representations (Ackerman 2003; Gibson 1969, 2000) or to other cultural contexts that use different types of discipline discourse (Carraher and Schliemann 2002). Yet, these theoretically motivated arguments remain to be tested empirically. The question of transfer is interesting also with respect to differences between STEM domains. Furthermore, the question of whether visual and connectional fluency transfer across topics, domains, or representation types, is important because it may affect an educator’s decision to invest instructional time for representational competencies.

Finally, we need to consider potential moderators of students’ acquisition of representational competencies. It is well established that spatial skills affect students’ learning with visual representations and their ability to acquire representational competencies (NRC 2006; Stieff 2007; Uttal et al. 2013). Integrating information from visual representations into students’ mental model of the content knowledge requires that students hold visual information in working memory and connect it to information in long-term memory (Hegarty and Waller 2005). Because spatial skills describe this very ability, cognitive load imposed by mental model integration is higher for students with low than with high spatial skills. Research on spatial skills has yielded instructional supports for spatial skills, but we do not yet know how spatial-skills supports interact with instructional supports for the representational competencies reviewed above.
Limitations

This review article has some limitations that should be noted. First, the review focused on visual representations that use purely perceptual devices as visual codes and that are encoded visually. Several types of representations do not meet these criteria because they use a combination of text-based and visual codes and are thus (at least in part) encoded verbally—such as maps, networks, matrices, or flow diagrams. We still know very little about how the use of such Bhybrid^ representations affects students’ learning. Future research should investigate how students’ understanding and fluency in using such representations affects their learning in STEM. In particular, hybrid representations often incorporate symbolic conventions that reoccur across multiple types of hybrid representations. Thus, students may have to understand and become fluent with symbolic conventions to process the visual aspects of hybrid representations. Another interesting aspect of hybrid representations relates to sociocultural aspects. Some STEM domains rely on hybrid representations more so than others (e.g., flow diagrams are common in computer sciences). It would be interesting to map out the types of text-based, visual, and hybrid representations used in various domains because that would allow us to conduct research on how the use of hybrid representations affects students use of visual representations and vice versa. To the extent that hybrid representations incorporate the same visual codes as some purely visual representations, understanding and fluency with hybrid representations may enhance students’ understanding and fluency with visual representations, thereby enhancing how they benefit from multiple visual representations overall. One might also argue that understanding and fluency with visual representations may enhance students’ benefit from hybrid representations.

Second, this article does not distinguish between different types of text-based representations. In most of the reviewed research, the text-based representation was written text. It may matter whether other types of text-based representations such as equations play a role during how students learn with visual representations. Future research should expand the space of scenarios covered in this article (see Fig. 1) to differentiate between single text-based and multiple text-based representations in addition to single and multiple visual representations.

A third related comment regards the focus on visualization-specific competencies, rather than general competencies such as spatial skills. For example, I consider the previously mentioned spatial skills as a general competency because they involve the ability to imagine and mentally transform any type of spatial information and to imagine any type of object from multiple perspectives in space (Hegarty and Waller 2005; NRC 2006). Although spatial skills play an important role in students’ learning with visual representations and predict students’ success in STEM (Hinze et al. 2013b; NRC 2006), they are not at the focus of this article because they are not tied to specific visual representations (e.g., understanding a pie chart versus understanding a numberline) but can transfer across a wide range of visual representations (Uttal et al. 2013). For an extensive review of research on spatial skills, refer to (Uttal et al. 2013).

Finally, this article assumes that most learners are fluent readers. International assessments such as PISA illustrate that this is a simplifying assumption that may not always hold (NCES 2011; OECD 2010). I am not aware of research that has investigated the effects of reading fluency on students’ learning with visual representations, but this would be an interesting area for future research. For example, do students who are not fluent readers engage more willingly with visual representations? Can visual fluency help students acquire fluency in reading?
Conclusions

Visual representations can help students learn, but they can also confuse students because students often have to learn new content from new visual representations they do not yet fully understand (called the Brepresentation dilemma^). To learn content knowledge from visual representations, students therefore need representational competencies: knowledge about how visual representations depict information about the content. Multimedia learning theory has focused on prior representational competencies that are prerequisites to students’ learning from visual representations. This article extends multimedia learning research by integrating cognitive learning theories and socio-cultural theories to gain insights into the learning processes through which acquire representational competencies while they learn content knowledge. This review revealed a number of representational competencies that students acquire via socially mediated verbal sense-making processes and nonverbal inductive learning processes. The focus on these learning processes provided the basis for an analysis of how the presence of multiple versus single visual representations the role these competencies play during students’ learning of content knowledge. This analysis yielded seven hypotheses that describe conditions under which we may expect multiple visual representations to be more effective than a single visual representation for students’ learning of content knowledge. Finding that most evidence for these hypotheses is indirect, open questions about the conditions for the effectiveness of multiple visual representations were discussed. Considering these conditions in the design of learning activities will likely help instructors and students navigate the representation dilemma, help students learn from visual representations, and thereby help them succeed in STEM.
